fields.Front: How do packet delay and loss arise at a router? What three things does the slide's router picture show?
fields.Back:
Packets queue in router buffers waiting for the output link; when the arrival rate temporarily exceeds the output link capacity the queue grows and, once the buffer is full, arriving packets are dropped.
Picture: 1) the packet being transmitted (transmission delay); 2) packets waiting in buffers (queueing delay); 3) free buffer space, without which arrivals are lost.

fields.Front: List the four sources of nodal delay, saying what each one is and what it depends on.
fields.Back:
1) d_proc, processing: check bit errors, look up output link; depends on router speed; typically < 1 ms (microseconds).
2) d_queue, queueing: wait at output link for turn; depends on router congestion (packets ahead); varies packet to packet.
3) d_trans, transmission: push L bits onto link; L/R; depends on packet length and link rate.
4) d_prop, propagation: travel to far end; d/s; depends on distance and medium.

fields.Front: What is queueing delay, what does it depend on, and why is it described statistically?
fields.Back:
Time a packet waits at the output link for its turn to be transmitted.
Depends on the congestion level of the router: zero if the queue is empty, long if many packets are ahead.
It is the only one of the four delays that varies from packet to packet under the same conditions, so we use averages, variance, and the probability of exceeding a threshold (governed by traffic intensity La/R).

fields.Front: Contrast transmission and propagation delay: what does each depend on, and what happens to each if you double the link rate?
fields.Back:
d_trans = L/R depends on packet length and link rate, not distance: doubling R halves it.
d_prop = d/s depends on distance and medium, not packet size or rate: doubling R leaves it unchanged.
On a long link propagation dominates; on a short LAN transmission dominates. Confusing them is the classic Chapter 1 error.

fields.Front: Numeric: a 1,500-byte packet, (a) on a 10 Mbps link 1,000 km long and (b) on a 1 Gbps LAN cable 10 m long (s = 2 x 10^8 m/s). Find d_trans and d_prop in each case, and say which dominates.
fields.Back:
L = 1,500 x 8 = 12,000 bits.
(a) d_trans = 12,000 / 10^7 = 1.2 ms; d_prop = 10^6 / (2 x 10^8) = 5 ms -> propagation dominates on a long link.
(b) d_trans = 12,000 / 10^9 = 12 microseconds; d_prop = 10 / (2 x 10^8) = 0.05 microseconds -> transmission dominates on a short fast LAN.

fields.Front: Numeric: how long to transmit a 1,500-byte packet onto a 100 Mbps link?
fields.Back:
L = 1,500 x 8 = 12,000 bits.
d_trans = 12,000 / 10^8 = 1.2 x 10^-4 s = 0.12 ms = 120 microseconds.
(Remember to convert bytes to bits.)

fields.Front: Numeric: a 2,000 km fiber link with s = 2 x 10^8 m/s. What is d_prop, and does it change if the link rate is doubled?
fields.Back:
d_prop = 2 x 10^6 m / (2 x 10^8 m/s) = 0.01 s = 10 ms.
No change: propagation delay depends only on distance and medium, never on the link's transmission rate.

fields.Front: In the caravan analogy, what do a car, the ten-car caravan, and a toll booth represent, and why must the whole caravan line up before the booth serves it?
fields.Back:
Car = bit; ten-car caravan = 10-bit packet; toll booth = router; highway segment = link.
The booth services one car at a time (bit transmission time) and only starts after the whole caravan has arrived: this models store-and-forward, where a router receives the entire packet before forwarding it.

fields.Front: Numeric (caravan case 1): cars propagate at 100 km/h, the booth takes 12 s per car, booths are 100 km apart. How long until the ten-car caravan is lined up at the 2nd booth?
fields.Back:
Time to push the caravan through the booth = 10 cars x 12 s = 120 s = 2 min (transmission delay).
Time for the last car to drive 100 km = 100 km / 100 km/h = 1 h (propagation delay).
Total = 62 minutes.

fields.Front: Numeric (caravan case 2): cars propagate at 1,000 km/h and the booth takes 1 min per car. Do cars reach the 2nd booth before all ten are serviced at the 1st?
fields.Back:
Yes. Driving 100 km takes 6 min; servicing all cars takes 10 min.
First car leaves at 1 min and arrives at the 2nd booth at 1 + 6 = 7 min, when 7 cars have been served and 3 are still at the 1st booth.
Lesson: a packet's first bits can reach the next router while its tail is still being transmitted (whenever d_trans > d_prop).

fields.Front: Why is the average queueing delay 'infinite' when La/R > 1, and what actually happens in a real router?
fields.Back:
On average more bits arrive than the link can transmit, so the queue grows without bound and waiting time is unbounded.
In reality the buffer is finite: it overflows and packets are dropped (loss), so the symptom is loss plus maximal delay rather than literally infinite waiting.

fields.Front: Numeric: packets of 1,000 bits arrive at 500 packets/s to a 1 Mbps link. Traffic intensity? What if the rate rises to 1,200 packets/s?
fields.Back:
La/R = 1,000 x 500 / 1,000,000 = 0.5: moderate load, small but non-zero average queueing delay.
At 1,200 packets/s: 1.2 > 1 -> overload, the queue grows without bound and packets are lost.
Compare 2,000-bit packets at 400 packets/s on the same link: La/R = 0.8, heavily loaded - a modest rise pushes it toward 1 where delay explodes.

fields.Front: Numeric: L = 1,000 bits, R = 10 Mbps. What average arrival rate a makes the traffic intensity exactly 1?
fields.Back:
Set La/R = 1, so a = R / L = 10^7 / 1,000 = 10,000 packets/s.
Any sustained arrival rate above this overloads the link; a good design keeps a well below it.

fields.Front: What causes packet loss at a router, and what are the three possible fates of a lost packet?
fields.Back:
The queue (buffer) before a link has finite capacity; a packet arriving to a full queue is dropped (lost). Loss fraction rises with traffic intensity, so nodes are judged by loss probability as well as delay.
A lost packet may be 1) retransmitted by the previous node, 2) retransmitted by the source end system (TCP's approach), or 3) not retransmitted at all.

fields.Front: Numeric: 3 links (2 routers), L = 1,500 bytes, R = 10 Mbps on every link, each link 100 km (s = 2 x 10^8 m/s), d_proc = 1 ms, no queueing. End-to-end delay?
What unit-conversion mistakes most often wreck delay calculations?
fields.Back:
1) Bytes vs bits: multiply bytes by 8 before L/R.
2) Prefixes: Kbit = 10^3, Mbps = 10^6, Gbps = 10^9 (a 10 Kbit packet on 100 Mbps takes 0.1 ms, not 0.1 s).
3) Distance: convert km to m before dividing by 2 x 10^8 m/s.
4) Time: keep seconds until the end, then convert to ms or microseconds.

fields.Front: Textbook only: what is Traceroute, how does it work, and what two things should you notice in real output? (Kurose §1.4.3)
fields.Back:
Traceroute runs on any host and reconstructs both the route and the round-trip delay to every router on it. The source sends special packets marked 1, 2, 3, ...; every router that receives one decrements the marking and forwards it, but a router at which the marking reaches zero stops and sends a short message back naming itself. The source times each reply. It repeats each measurement three times, so it sends 3N packets for N-1 intervening routers (RFC 1393).
In real output: (1) the delay JUMPS sharply at one hop when the path crosses a long link - a transatlantic fibre link shows up as a jump from ~7 ms to ~78 ms; (2) delays are NOT monotonic - a later router can report a smaller delay than an earlier one, because queueing delay varies with time. An asterisk means a probe was lost.

fields.Front: Textbook only: give the typical magnitude of each of the four delays, and name two delays that happen inside the end system. (Kurose §1.4.1, §1.4.3)
fields.Back:
d_proc: microseconds or less in high-speed routers - usually negligible in a calculation, but it sets the router's maximum forwarding throughput.
d_queue: microseconds to milliseconds; the only one that varies packet to packet.
d_trans: microseconds to milliseconds.
d_prop: microseconds on a campus link, milliseconds across a WAN, hundreds of milliseconds over a geostationary satellite. Propagation speed is 2 x 10^8 to 3 x 10^8 m/s.
Inside the end system: (1) a host on a shared medium (WiFi, cable) may deliberately delay transmitting as part of the multiple access protocol; (2) media packetization delay - a video-conferencing sender must fill a packet with encoded video and speech before it can hand it to the network at all.

fields.Text: Nodal processing delay d_proc: time to {{c1::check bit errors}} and {{c1::determine the output link}} (forwarding-table lookup); typically {{c1::under a millisecond}} (microseconds in fast routers).

Transmission delay d_trans = {{c1::L / R}}: L = {{c1::packet length in bits}}, R = {{c1::link transmission rate in bps}}; it is the time to push all bits onto the link and is independent of {{c1::link length (distance)}}.

Propagation delay d_prop = {{c1::d / s}}: d = {{c1::length of the physical link (m)}}, s = {{c1::propagation speed in the medium (~2 x 10^8 m/s)}}; time for one bit to cross the link, independent of {{c1::packet length and link rate}}.

Traffic intensity = {{c1::L x a / R}}: L = {{c1::packet length (bits)}}, a = {{c1::average packet arrival rate (packets/s)}}, R = {{c1::link bandwidth (bps)}}; L x a is the average bit arrival rate, so the ratio is the fraction of capacity demanded.

Traffic intensity = {{c1::La/R}}. Near 0 the average queueing delay is {{c1::small}}; approaching 1 it grows {{c1::rapidly toward infinity}}; above 1 the queue grows {{c1::without bound}}. Golden rule: design so La/R is {{c1::no greater than 1}}. Even below 1, {{c1::periodic}} arrivals never queue while {{c1::bursty}} ones make the nth packet of a burst wait {{c1::(n-1)L/R}}.
A packet arriving to a {{c1::full buffer (queue)}} is dropped. A lost packet may be retransmitted by the {{c1::previous node}}, by the {{c1::source end system}}, or {{c1::not at all}}.

End-to-end delay with N-1 routers (N identical links, no queueing): d_end-end = {{c1::N x (d_proc + d_trans + d_prop)}}, with d_trans = {{c1::L/R}}; it generalizes {{c1::N x L/R}}; with queueing add each node's {{c1::d_queue}} inside the parentheses.
